While defects are managed differently from one project to the next, the component parts found in an approach for defining how defects are managed is fairly consistent. Each project defines the contents of the component parts differently depending on factors such as project complexity, size, cost and scope. Component parts to define an approach for managing defects are highlighted in the following sections:

Defect status meetings

A common practice performed over the life of a project is to schedule regular meetings to communicate new defects, to discuss status of existing defects, to analyze defect trends, and to prioritize the defects in order to allocate resources and resolve issues in a timely a manner. Defect status meetings are typically held at regular intervals but may increase in frequency during testing of the target solution.

Defect management tool selection

In order to properly generate metrics and confirm consistent defect tracking, a defect tracking database or repository is utilized. Many test management tools have capabilities to assist management of defects. Critical functions of a test management tool required for tracking and managing defects include:

  • Allocates or records a unique identifier for the incident
  • Captures a full defect description to facilitate reproduction during prioritization for resolution and debugging
  • Tracks the defect status as the defect progresses in an appropriate sequence from identification to resolution
  • Provides functionality to report key defect metrics by project and across all projects
  • Web based and available to all authorized users

Defect resolution process

Typically defined in a visual illustration, a defect resolution process defines a systematic sequence of steps to resolve defects in a timely manner. The process also defines hand-offs between roles and the differing responsibilities involved in resolving defects. A common practice is to associate a status for each step in the process. The defect's status is updated to reflect progress from defect identification to defect resolution as the defect flows through the process. The following is an example of a set of statuses for a resolution process:

  • New
    • A defect is logged and routed for secondary review
  • Analysis
    • A defect is analyzed to determine validity
    • Valid defects are assigned a priority, severity and classification
  • Open
    • A valid defect is opened and handed to development for a resolution
  • In development
    • A development team is working towards a resolution for the defect
  • Fixed
    • A defect is corrected and is in unit test
  • Retest
    • New code with a defect resolution has been migrated to the appropriate test environment waiting for a retest
  • Reopened
    • Defect is retested and the defect remains unresolved
  • Closed
    • Defect is retested and resolution is validated
  • Canceled
    • Defect has been withdrawn

Defect documentation

A defect is logged any time a test script fails to meet the expected results. Details recorded about each defect occurrence include, but are not limited to, the following information:

  • Description of the defect
  • Associated requirements and test scripts
  • Defect consequences
  • Sequence of steps to re-create the defect
  • Perceived severity and when available
  • Error logs

Documenting details of a defect is important to allow for a productive discussion on proper defect analysis.

Defect analysis

Review of defects after initial identification is a common practice and identification and analysis of defects are usually segregated responsibilities. An independent review is performed to verify the validity of defects identified. In some cases, defects may be re-classified and closed as non-defects. Non-defects are often classified as the following:

  • Irreproducible
  • Duplicate defect
  • Enhancement or change request
  • Out of scope
  • Issue or risk
    • In some situations, discovered defects may not have a viable resolution. For example, a defect for a feature whose only resolution negatively impacts - or in worst case breaks - the functionality of a software application is often deemed unfixable. These defects are reclassified as risks or issues and escalated to stakeholders for further review. Stakeholders evaluate the known risks and issues when deciding to transition to the target solution. Stakeholders must determine whether to transition to the target solution knowing the risks and issues.

Analyzing duplicates or other non-defect may provide insight into duplicated testing efforts or incorrect script creation. Once verified, defects are commonly assigned a severity, priority and classification.

Defect severity

The severity indicates the degree of negative impact a defect has on the functionality and quality of the target solution. In other words, the severity is determined by the importance of the functionality in relation to the requirements. Severity terminology and definitions typically vary from one project to the next. The following is an example of defect severity levels and definitions:

Severity Definition
Critical Target solution does not meet minimal acceptable functionality. The defect causes a system crash or corruption of critical information; the function cannot be performed, or testing cannot continue. A workaround does not exist.
High Significant impact on ability to complete objectives on time. Defect results in severely impaired functionality. A workaround may exist but is unsatisfactory or cumbersome.
Medium Impact is manageable and easily deployable workaround exists. Defect produces incorrect, incomplete or inconsistent results or impairs usability. The level of adjustments required is manageable.
Low A workaround for the defect exists and can be supported for more than one occurrence. The target solution does not conform to normal standards or is related to the aesthetics of the system. The level of adjustments required is minimal.

Defect priority

Defects are assigned a priority based on its impact to the critical path of the project. Assigning a priority indicates how quickly the defect must be repaired and assists appropriate allocation of resources for defect resolution. A service-level agreement that defines the turnaround time to resolve a defect often complements a defect priority rating. The following is an example of defect priority ratings, definitions and associated turnaround times:

Priority Definition Expected turnaround
Critical The defect must be fixed immediately to avoid loss of functionality, financial liability, or negative impact on development of other areas in the target solution.
  • 8 hours
  • Resolve immediately
  • All other defects are placed on hold until the critical priority defects are resolved
High The defect must be addressed in the current release, or a workaround evaluated.
  • 8-24 hours
  • Resolve as soon as all other critical defects are resolved
Medium There is minimal liability or additional development risks or costs. The defect can be fixed in the next or subsequent code migration.
  • Greater than 24 hours
  • Resolve after all critical and high priority defects are resolved.
Low Resolution is designated for a future release.
  • Prior to completion of the test effort
  • Resolution of this defect is labeled as "nice to have."

Defect classification

Defects classification, also sometimes referred to as the root-cause analysis, is performed in order to drive metrics and understand the reasoning behind groupings of defects in a project. Classifying the defect can be difficult and is not critical for resolution. However, a generally accepted practice is to classify all defects prior to closing. Categories for defect classification vary depending on the type of testing performed. The following is an example classification of defects during application software testing:

Classification Definition
Coding error A defect caused by improper development
Configuration error A defect caused by incorrect settings in the application
Incorrect requirements A defect created by a misunderstood or missed requirement
Works as designed Defect is not valid, and system is working as designed
User error User did not use the system or application correctly
Workflow logic A defect caused by an incorrect workflow
Issue or risk A defect that cannot be resolved and needs to be addressed by stakeholders

Defect metrics and reporting

Detailed reporting of defect metrics is critical to projects success. Defect metrics are important for identifying trends and predicting patterns over the course of the test effort. Should defect metrics indicate a potential risk or issue, stakeholders may elect to adjust project timelines, processes and allocation of resources thereby reducing project costs and minimizing project risks. For example, in an adequately staffed project, defect rates rise quickly, peak somewhere in the middle of the test effort and slowly decrease as the project concludes. If defect rates are still rising in the third week of a four-week test effort, then the project is likely not on schedule and stakeholder may elect to increase the number of resources or extend the length of the test effort. In other instances, a low rate of closed defects may indicate a lack of resources to fix and retest defects.

There are three main classes of meaningful defect metric reports:

  1. Defect density or distribution reports
    • These reports illustrate how long a defect has existed in a particular state in the defect management process (e.g., the number of days a defect has been in "Open" status).
  2. Defect age reports
    • These reports illustrate how long a defect has existed in a particular state in the defect management process (e.g., the number of days a defect has been in "Open" status).
  3. Defect trend reports
    • These reports show defect counts as a function of time. This analysis helps stakeholders identify various rates which indicate how quickly solution quality is improving over the course of the test effort.
